why.why: Classic bilateral periorbital purpura without trauma, carpal tunnel syndrome, and familial cardiac death already suggested systemic amyloidosis. Expert analyses now confirm hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis: genetic testing shows pathogenic TTR Ala19Asp variant, cardiac imaging shows amyloid cardiomyopathy with apical sparing, and nuclear scintigraphy shows grade 3 cardiac uptake. These findings make systemic amyloidosis nearly certain. Elevated free light chain ratio without monoclonal protein argues against AL subtype but does not diminish the systemic amyloidosis diagnosis.

focus.label: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR)
focus.why: The current frontier 'Systemic amyloidosis' is too general. The pathogenic TTR Ala19Asp variant (node-12), echocardiographic apical sparing (node-10), grade 3 nuclear scintigraphic uptake (node-11), and absence of monoclonal protein (node-9) all converge to support hereditary ATTR as the specific subtype of systemic amyloidosis.

payload.report: The five-year bilateral periorbital purpura without trauma, combined with echocardiographic apical sparing, grade 3 nuclear scintigraphic uptake, and a pathogenic TTR Ala19Asp variant, strongly supports hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR). The purpura is best explained by amyloid infiltration of dermal vessels. Elevated free light chains without monoclonal protein argues against AL amyloidosis, and no chronic inflammatory disease supports AA amyloidosis. Bleeding disorders, traumatic purpura, and age-related vascular fragility are effectively excluded. Confidence is 0.96, pending Congo red histopathological confirmation.
